questions.stem:
The reception starts with toasts to the couple. A wedding toast is a custom where a close friend or relative of the groom or the bride says a few words to wish the couple, then everyone raises their glass of wine, and drink it up at the same moment. The groom is then asked to kiss the bride. After a few toasts, people start eating and drinking, and generally have fun.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write a speech (100 words) for your school assembly on the topic ‘Customs of a Russian Wedding’, describing what a Russian wedding involves and how the groom fetches the bride for the registration.

markingPoints.description: Format: opens with a greeting to the audience and closes with a thank-you, and stays within about 100 words (1)
Content: says a Russian wedding is very simple and its planning includes only rings, a bride’s dress, cars and a reception, with the bride’s and groom’s families sharing the expenses (1)
Content: gives the length of a wedding — two days, and some as long as a week — and the friends’ preparations of posters, speeches and contests (1)
Content: describes the procession of several cars, and the groom climbing several stairs, answering a question at each landing and paying cash if he guesses wrong (1)
Organisation and expression: presents the customs in a clear order in simple, accurate sentences (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Good morning everyone. A Russian wedding is very simple. The planning includes only rings, a bride’s dress, cars and a reception, and the bride’s and groom’s families now share the expenses. A wedding lasts two days; some last as long as a week. The best friends of the couple meet a few times before it to make posters, write speeches and organise contests. A procession of several cars is a necessary part. When the groom comes to fetch the bride for the registration, he must climb several stairs and answer a question at every landing. If he guesses wrong, he pays cash. Thank you.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write an article (100 words) for your school magazine on the theme ‘Why quarrelling did not stop the proposal’, giving the reason the two families wanted the marriage and showing how the proposal was nearly forgotten.

markingPoints.description: Format: gives the article a suitable heading, keeps to about 100 words and presents the matter as connected prose (1)
Content: states that the play is about wealthy families seeking ties with other wealthy families to increase their estates by encouraging marriages that make good economic sense (1)
Content: names Ivan Lomov as the long time wealthy neighbour who comes to seek the hand of Stepan Chubukov’s twenty-five-year-old daughter, Natalya (1)
Content: explains that all three are quarrelsome and quarrel over petty issues, so the proposal is in danger of being forgotten (1)
Content and expression: closes by saying economic good sense ensures that the proposal is made, although the quarrelling perhaps continues, and links cause to effect clearly (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Why Quarrelling Did Not Stop the Proposal
The one-act farce The Proposal is about the tendency of wealthy families to seek ties with other wealthy families, to increase their estates by encouraging marriages that make good economic sense. Ivan Lomov, a long time wealthy neighbour of Stepan Chubukov, also wealthy, comes to seek the hand of Chubukov’s twenty-five-year-old daughter, Natalya. All three are quarrelsome people, and they quarrel over petty issues, so the proposal is in danger of being forgotten. Yet economic good sense ensures that the proposal is made, after all, although the quarrelling perhaps continues.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: A neighbour calling in evening dress and asking for a private word is enough to make a landowner suspect him; why does Chubukov first believe that Lomov has come to borrow money?

markingPoints.description: Notes that Lomov enters in a dress-jacket and white gloves, so the visit looks like a formal call rather than a courtship (1)
Notes that Chubukov comments on how formal Lomov’s get-up is and even compares it to paying a New Year’s Eve visit (1)
Gives his aside — ‘He’s come to borrow money. Shan’t give him any!’ — as the reason he expects a loan request and is unwilling to help (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Chubukov reads the visit as a request for cash, not for his daughter’s hand. Lomov has walked in wearing a dress-jacket and white gloves, and Chubukov at once complains that he is formal in his get-up and asks whether he is paying a New Year’s Eve visit. His aside settles his mind: ‘He’s come to borrow money. Shan’t give him any!’

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: A visitor waiting to be called in trembles as though he had an examination before him; why does Lomov feel he must have his mind made up at once?

markingPoints.description: States that Lomov is trembling all over, as if he had an examination before him (1)
Gives his reason: if he gives himself time to think, to hesitate, to talk a lot, or to look for an ideal or for real love, then he will never marry (1)
Adds that he is already 35, a critical age, and that it is impossible for him not to marry (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Lomov is trembling all over and says the great thing is that he must have his mind made up. He is sure that if he gives himself time to think, to hesitate, to talk a lot, or to look for an ideal or for real love, then he’ll never get married. So he fixes on proposing while his nerve lasts; he also says he is already 35, a critical age, and it is impossible for him not to marry.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Two neighbouring families, who say they have always been affectionate towards each other, end up arguing over the same plot of land; why does each side claim the Oxen Meadows?

markingPoints.description: Gives Lomov’s side: the Meadows are wedged in between the Chubukovs’ birchwoods and the Burnt Marsh (1)

Adds his family’s right: his aunt’s grandmother gave the free use of the Meadows in perpetuity to the peasants of Natalya’s grandfather, who had them for forty years and then regarded them as their own (1)
Gives Natalya’s side: both grandfather and great-grandfather reckoned that their land extended to Burnt Marsh, which makes the Meadows theirs (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Lomov claims the Meadows because they are wedged in between the Chubukovs’ birchwoods and the Burnt Marsh, and because his aunt’s grandmother gave the free use of them in perpetuity to the peasants of Natalya’s grandfather, who used them for forty years and then regarded them as their own. Natalya claims them because both grandfather and great-grandfather reckoned that their land extended to Burnt Marsh.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: A father hears a neighbour ask for his daughter’s hand and then embraces and kisses the man, saying he has always loved him as his own son; what makes Chubukov accept Lomov so completely?

He says this has been his continual desire for a long time, and that he has always loved Lomov as if he were his own son.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: A reader watches the same young woman turn from a courteous hostess into the person who ends the argument; trace in steps how Natalya’s manner changes from the moment the visitor sits down to the end of the dispute.

markingPoints.description: Step 1: shows the courteous start — she excuses her apron and neglige, mentions the shelling of peas for drying, and questions the evening dress (1)
Step 2: shows the friendly small talk about the weather and about the hay he has stacked, with an offer of lunch (1)
Step 3: shows the first real challenge, when she interrupts to ask whether the Meadows are his and then claims they are theirs, not his (1)
Step 4: notes her half-retreat, answering only that yes, they’re ours, when he describes the Meadows as wedged in between the birchwoods and the Burnt Marsh (1)
Step 5: notes that she presses him by asking how long they have been his and says she will not believe it (1)
Step 6: shows her closing the dispute — grandfather and great-grandfather reckoned their land reached the Burnt Marsh, so the Meadows were hers, and there is nothing to argue about (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — Courteous hostess: she excuses her apron and neglige, explains that they are shelling peas for drying, and asks why the visitor is in evening dress.
Step 2 — Idle talk: she asks him to sit down, offers him lunch, and chats about the weather and about how much hay he has stacked.
Step 3 — The first challenge: she interrupts him to ask whether the Oxen Meadows are really his, then flatly says that Oxen Meadows are theirs, not his.
Step 4 — A half-retreat: when he says they are wedged in between the birchwoods and the Burnt Marsh, she only answers that yes, they’re ours.
Step 5 — She presses him: she asks how long they have been his and says she will not be got to believe it.
Step 6 — She closes the argument: both grandfather and great-grandfather reckoned their land extended to Burnt Marsh, so the Meadows were ours, and she sees nothing to argue about.
